messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Violence: Violence, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Carlos sat forward in the chair, his thick, scarred hands resting on his knees. At seventy, he was still a powerfully built man, a lifetime of welding having left him with a frame that was all dense muscle and stubborn sinew. But his dark eyes, the color of wet earth, held a constant, searching vigilance. He had come to the clinic at the insistence of his daughter, who had found him, for the third time that month, standing frozen in the middle of the hardware store, unable to move or speak. He had been looking at a roll of chain-link fencing.

The event that had broken the world into a before and after happened forty-two years ago, in a small town outside of San Salvador. Carlos had been a union organizer, a quiet but effective man who could talk to the coffee workers in a way the landowners could not. One evening, three men in civilian clothes had pulled him from his home. They did not take him to a station. They took him to a concrete room beneath a warehouse, a room with a single, bare bulb and a drain in the center of the floor. For three days, they asked him questions about names and meeting places. For three days, he did not answer. They used electricity, they used water, and they used a thick, rusted length of rebar. The worst part, the part that lived in him still, was not the pain itself, but the sound of the rebar whistling before it hit, and the complete, suffocating certainty that he had no options. There was no door he could open, no bargain he could strike, no god he could pray to that would stop the next swing. He was a container for their violence, and the only choice he had was to endure.

The memory of that room did not feel like a memory. When it came, it was not a story he recalled; it was a room he was suddenly inside. The smell of damp concrete would fill his nostrils while he was checking the pressure on an acetylene tank. The particular weight of a hand on his shoulder from a coworker would make his whole body lock, the present moment dissolving into the feeling of being bound. He could never explain this to anyone. When his daughter asked him what was wrong, the words would tangle in his throat. The thread of the narrative would vanish, and he would be left with nothing but the image of the bare bulb and the sound of his own ragged breathing, and he would simply stop talking.

He had developed a quiet, desperate system for survival. He tried hard not to think about it. He would catch himself beginning to drift toward that room and he would mentally slam a door, focusing instead on the precise heat of his welding torch or the number of stitches in a seam. He had also become, over the decades, a man who said yes to everything. When a foreman barked an unreasonable order, Carlos would nod and comply. When a neighbor asked for a favor that cost him his entire Saturday, he would agree without a thought. He had learned that the safest way to exist was to be invisible and agreeable. His body had learned that resistance was what got you beaten. So he smiled, he complied, and he seethed. The rage was a constant, low-frequency hum beneath the compliance. When he did remember—when the mental door failed to slam shut—the rage was not a flash of anger. It was a deep, oceanic fury that terrified him. He was certain that if he ever let it out, he would not be able to stop.

He lived in a state of permanent threat assessment. He had come to believe, with the bone-deep certainty of a man who has been proven right, that you can never know who will harm you. The man in the pickup truck at the gas station could be one of them. The new supervisor at the fabrication shop had a certain way of standing that made Carlos’s skin prickle. Every stranger was a potential interrogator. He was also certain that the whole thing was his fault. He blamed himself for the way he had acted—for the fact that he had not fought back harder, that he had not found a way to escape, that he had not done more to stop what happened. This guilt was a cold, hard stone in his gut. He would never forgive himself for his own inaction, for the fact that he had survived while others, he was sure, had not.

The consequences had accumulated slowly, like rust. He had outlived his wife by eight years, but he had never been able to be present for her. She had learned not to touch him from behind. He had lost contact with his old friends from the union; they reminded him of a person he no longer was. His job as a welder, the one place he had felt competent and in control, had become a minefield. The high-pitched hiss of a gas line could sound like a gunshot. The clang of a dropped steel beam was a gunshot. The sound of a car backfiring in the parking lot was always, always a gunshot. He would drop his helmet and stand perfectly still, his heart hammering, his mind returning to that concrete room where the only sound was the one that preceded the pain.

What had finally brought him here was not the fear, but the loneliness. He had been standing in his empty kitchen, staring at the stove, unable to decide whether to make coffee because the decision felt as impossible as choosing which bone to break first. He had realized that he was not living. He was just waiting. He was waiting for the next bad thing, the next trigger, the next time the past would swallow the present. He was terrified of what he might find in therapy—terrified that he would have to open the door to that room and look at it directly. But he was more terrified of the alternative. He was hoping, with a small, fragile part of himself that he had thought was dead, that someone could teach him how to stop holding his breath.
